title: Networking Essentials
summary: Every arrow has a cost. Learn how DNS, TCP, UDP, TLS, HTTP versions, API styles, L4/L7 balancing and connection reuse change your design.
body:
Every arrow on a system design diagram is a network call, and each one has a cost: name resolution, connection setup, encryption, serialization and distance. Interviewers rarely ask you to recite the TCP state machine, but they do expect you to choose sensible protocols for clients and services, place load balancers at the right layer, explain why a real-time feature uses WebSockets instead of polling, and account for latency when users are far from your servers. This lesson covers the networking facts that actually change designs.

## What happens before the first byte

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant C as Client
    participant R as DNS resolver
    participant E as Edge or load balancer
    participant S as Service
    C->>R: Resolve api.example.com
    R-->>C: IP address with TTL
    C->>E: TCP SYN
    E-->>C: SYN-ACK
    C->>E: ACK plus TLS ClientHello
    E-->>C: TLS ServerHello and certificate
    C->>E: HTTP request
    E->>S: Forward over pooled connection
    S-->>E: Response
    E-->>C: Response
```

A cold request pays for DNS (often cached), one round trip for the TCP handshake, one more for a TLS 1.3 handshake, and only then the request itself. At a 150 ms round trip, that is roughly 450 ms before the server does any work. The edge forwards to the service over an already-open connection, so the internal hop costs only a fraction of a millisecond. Reusing connections and terminating TLS close to the user are the two largest latency wins in most systems.

## DNS

DNS maps names to addresses through a hierarchy: a recursive resolver asks root, top-level-domain and authoritative servers, then caches the answer for its time-to-live (TTL). Two consequences matter in design. First, DNS can steer traffic: geographic or latency-based DNS returns the nearest region's address, and weighted records shift traffic gradually. Second, DNS failover is slow and imprecise: resolvers and clients may cache an answer beyond its TTL, so pointing a name at a new region can take minutes to propagate fully. Use low TTLs (30–60 s) where you need agility, and prefer anycast or a global load balancer when failover must be fast.

## TCP and UDP

TCP provides an ordered, reliable byte stream with flow and congestion control. It costs a handshake and suffers head-of-line blocking: one lost packet stalls all data behind it on that connection until it is retransmitted. UDP sends independent datagrams with no handshake, ordering or retransmission. Applications choose UDP when late data is useless (live voice, game state) or when they implement their own reliability, as QUIC does. "UDP is faster" is only true if you can tolerate or handle loss yourself.

## TLS

TLS authenticates the server (and optionally the client) with certificates and encrypts traffic. TLS 1.3 needs one round trip for a full handshake and supports 0-RTT resumption, which lets a returning client send data immediately; that early data can be replayed by an attacker, so only allow it for idempotent requests. Inside a datacenter, mutual TLS between services is a common zero-trust default. Terminating TLS at the load balancer lets it inspect HTTP, but traffic beyond that point is plaintext unless you re-encrypt.

## HTTP versions

| Version | Transport | Key property | Limitation |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| HTTP/1.1 | TCP | Keep-alive reuses connections | One in-flight request per connection in practice; browsers open several connections |
| HTTP/2 | TCP | Many concurrent streams on one connection; header compression | A lost TCP packet still blocks every stream |
| HTTP/3 | QUIC over UDP | Streams recover from loss independently; combined transport and TLS handshake; connection migration across networks | UDP is sometimes blocked or rate-limited; more CPU per byte today |

HTTP/3 helps most on lossy mobile networks. Inside a datacenter, HTTP/2 over long-lived connections is usually sufficient.

## API styles in one table

| Style | Strength | Weakness | Typical use |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| REST over HTTP/JSON | Universal tooling, cacheable GETs, easy debugging | Over- or under-fetching; loosely typed | Public and browser-facing APIs |
| gRPC (HTTP/2, Protocol Buffers) | Typed contracts, compact encoding, streaming, generated clients | Weak browser support without a proxy; binary payloads harder to inspect | Service-to-service calls |
| GraphQL | Clients select exactly the fields they need across a graph | Harder HTTP caching; expensive queries need depth and cost limits | Aggregating many backends for varied clients |

For real-time server-to-client updates, plain request/response is not enough. Long polling holds a request open until data arrives; Server-Sent Events stream one-way text over HTTP; WebSockets upgrade to a full-duplex connection. Each long-lived connection consumes memory on a server, so you need connection-aware load balancing and a way to route a message to the server holding a user's socket.

## Load balancers, proxies and gateways

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    U["Users"] --> DNS["Geo DNS"]
    DNS --> CDN["CDN edge (static, TLS)"]
    CDN --> L4["L4 balancer (TCP)"]
    L4 --> GW["L7 gateway (auth, rate limit, routing)"]
    GW --> A["Orders service"]
    GW --> B["Search service"]
    A --> DB[("Orders DB")]
    B --> IDX[("Search index")]
```

DNS sends users to a nearby region, the CDN serves cacheable content and terminates TLS near the user, an L4 balancer spreads TCP connections across gateway instances, and the L7 gateway makes per-request decisions before forwarding to services. Not every system needs every layer; a small service may use one managed L7 balancer.

An **L4** balancer routes by IP and port and forwards connections without parsing HTTP. It is fast and protocol-agnostic but cannot route by path or header, and with HTTP/2 it balances connections, not requests. An **L7** balancer parses HTTP, so it can route by path, retry idempotent requests, apply canary weights and spread individual requests across backends, at the cost of terminating TLS and more CPU. A **reverse proxy** sits in front of servers (NGINX, Envoy); a **forward proxy** sits in front of clients, for example an egress proxy that controls outbound calls. An **API gateway** is an L7 reverse proxy with product features: authentication, rate limiting, request transformation and API keys. Keep business logic out of it.

## Keep-alive and connection pooling

Opening a connection per request wastes round trips and CPU, and at high rates can exhaust ephemeral ports. Clients and services should hold pools of persistent connections. Databases are the sharpest case: each PostgreSQL connection is a server process, so 200 app instances × 50 connections is 10,000 processes, which is far more than a primary should run. Put a pooler such as PgBouncer in between, or size pools to the database rather than to the app fleet. Long-lived pooled connections also defeat L4 balancing after scaling out, because old connections stay on old backends; set a maximum connection age so traffic rebalances.

## Regions and latency

Serving users from one region means distant users pay intercontinental round trips on every uncached request. Options, in order of complexity: put static assets and cacheable reads on a CDN; terminate TLS at edge locations so handshakes are short; run read replicas in other regions; and finally run multi-region writes, which forces conflict resolution or a per-record home region. Most designs should state a primary region, edge caching, and a disaster-recovery region, then justify anything more.

## Failure modes and interview mistakes

- Treating a network call like a function call: every remote call needs a timeout, and retries need limits and idempotency.
- Assuming DNS failover is instant.
- Choosing L4 load balancing for HTTP/2 or gRPC traffic and then wondering why one backend is hot: long-lived multiplexed connections pin load.
- Proposing WebSockets without explaining how a message finds the server holding the recipient's connection.
- Ignoring connection limits on databases when scaling the app tier.

## How to use it in an interview

Name protocols at boundaries: "Clients use HTTPS with REST; internal services use gRPC; live updates use WebSockets through a connection gateway." Quote the latency that matters: a cross-region synchronous write adds ~100 ms. Expect follow-ups on where TLS terminates, how a sticky connection rebalances after a deploy, and what happens when a region fails.

## Interview exercise

Users in Sydney complain that your US-hosted dashboard takes two seconds to load, with 20 API calls per page. Estimate how much of that is round-trip time, then list three changes in order of effort, and say which network property each one exploits.

## Further reading

- [MDN: An overview of HTTP](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Overview) covers connections, HTTP versions and caching semantics.
- [RFC 9000: QUIC](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9000) specifies the transport beneath HTTP/3.
- [gRPC documentation](https://grpc.io/docs/) describes the RPC model, streaming and HTTP/2 transport.
keyTakeaways: A cold HTTPS request costs roughly three round trips before the server responds; reuse connections and terminate TLS near users.
DNS can steer users to regions, but cached answers make DNS failover slow and imprecise.
HTTP/2 multiplexes streams over one TCP connection; HTTP/3 over QUIC removes cross-stream head-of-line blocking.
L4 balancers route connections; L7 balancers route requests and are needed to spread multiplexed HTTP/2 or gRPC traffic.
Pool connections, especially to databases, and plan how long-lived connections rebalance after scaling.
